owner: CC gates writes to cairn/devices/ground_loop/ (charter's gated_by).
intention: When a second ground loop starts, it reads the running loop's last device list. If that list is more than 120s old, the newcomer kills the stale loop and takes over. If it is fresh, the newcomer exits — the running loop is healthy and needs no replacement.
why: The double-loop incident (2026-08-18, 80 minutes) had both halves of the answer on disk the whole time and nothing looked. The flock/inode approach in guard.py is replaced by this: the device list the loop already writes is the liveness signal, and 120s is the staleness threshold (Akien, 2026-08-25). No new file, no lock, no /proc — one stat on something the loop already produces.
how: On startup, before entering the beat loop: read the timestamp on the running loop's last device list. If age > 120s, kill the old process (its pid is in the liveness file) and proceed as the new loop. If age <= 120s, exit cleanly — the running loop is alive. The device list and the pid are both already written by the existing beat; no new state file needed.
traces_to: Law 4 — a rule that matters is enforced by physics, not policy. The single-loop invariant was prose in guard.py's docstring; this makes it a startup check.
Law 10 — nothing inside is beyond measuring. Both signals (device-list age, pid) were on the machine for the whole incident and nothing read them together.
falsifier: RED on any of: (1) two loops run simultaneously for more than one beat cycle — the core property; (2) a healthy loop (device list < 120s old) is killed by a newcomer — the newcomer should exit, not fight; (3) a stale loop (device list > 120s old) survives when a newcomer starts — the newcomer should take over; (4) the arbitration requires any file the beat does not already write — no new state.
children: none — the mechanism is one age check and one conditional kill at startup, leaf-sized
